sec: Potassium Metabolism · Na+/K+ ATPase, regulation, severity rules and renal handling

items.q: What does the page credit the Na+/K+ ATPase with doing for potassium?
opts: Accumulating K+ intracellularly against its electrochemical gradient
Exchanging intracellular Na+ for extracellular K+ down its gradient
Pumping K+ into the tubular lumen for excretion
Binding K+ to intracellular proteins for storage
items.exp: The first bullet states that the pump helps in intracellular accumulation of K+ against its electrochemical gradient. (Book p969)

items.q: Assess the digoxin bullets: I Potassium and digoxin are said to share the same binding site on the Na+/K+ ATPase. II Because of that competition, digoxin is listed as a cause of hypokalemia.
items.exp: The shared binding-site statement is correct, but the next bullet states that digoxin leads to hyperkalemia, not hypokalemia. (Book p969)

items.q: A patient with a digoxin level of 4 ng/mL has a serum potassium of 2.6 mEq/L. Which action on this page is directly endorsed?
opts: Give furosemide to enhance digoxin clearance
items.exp: The page states that potassium can be given in digoxin toxicity, which fits the hypokalemic patient in whom low potassium worsens glycoside binding. (Book p969)

items.q: Fill up: Trained athletes maintain a higher intracellular potassium because of ______ activity of the skeletal muscle ______ pump.
items.exp: The last bullet attributes the athletic adaptation to increased activity of the skeletal muscle Na+/K+ ATPase, which maintains a raised intracellular K+. (Book p969)

items.q: Of the 100 mEq daily intake in the regulation flowchart, what proportion leaves through the kidneys and what proportion through the gut?
items.exp: The regulation tree splits the daily 100 mEq into 90-95% renal excretion and 5-10% through the GIT. (Book p969)

items.q: The tubular diagram states that the filtered load of potassium is about 700 mEq/day. What fraction of that load is excreted under normal conditions?
items.exp: The diagram notes that normal kidneys excrete 10-15% of the filtered load, after 70-80% paracellular reabsorption in the PCT and a further 10% via the TALH Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter. (Book p969)

items.q: Match each tubular segment with the potassium handling step drawn for it — 1) Proximal convoluted tubule 2) Thick ascending limb of Henle 3) Aldosterone-dependent collecting duct … A) 10% reabsorption through Na+/K+/2Cl- B) H+,K+-ATPase activity with secretion through ROMK C) 70-80% paracellular reabsorption
items.exp: Paracellular reabsorption of 70-80% is placed in the PCT, 10% is reclaimed at the TALH via Na+/K+/2Cl-, and the collecting duct carries the aldosterone-driven H+,K+-ATPase with luminal ROMK and a basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase. (Book p969)

items.q: The renal-excretion diagram at the thick ascending limb labels several structures. Which one is NOT part of that drawing?
opts: ROMK channel on the luminal membrane
items.exp: The drawing shows luminal ROMK with Na+, K+ and Cl- entries, a basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase and arrows for Ca2+ and Mg2+ reabsorption; no glucose cotransporter appears. (Book p969)

items.q: According to the severity rule on this page, hypokalemia below which range is called significant?
items.exp: Significant hypokalemia is under 2-2.5 mEq/L and is attributed to renal loss unless proven otherwise, while 2.5-3.5 mEq/L is the insignificant band attributed to cellular shift. (Book p969)

items.q: Apply the page's two severity rules: I A serum potassium of 2.2 mEq/L should be assumed to reflect renal loss. II A serum potassium of 3.1 mEq/L is labelled insignificant and blamed on a cellular shift.
items.exp: 2.2 mEq/L sits in the significant band where renal loss is the default, and 3.1 mEq/L sits in the insignificant band attributed to shift. (Book p969)

items.q: The page gives a parallel rule for significant hyperkalemia: it is attributed to which cause unless proven otherwise?
opts: Renal failure, with aldosterone named in brackets
Cellular shift, with beta-blockers named in brackets
Gastrointestinal loss, with diarrhoea named in brackets
Spurious haemolysis, with fist clenching named in brackets
items.exp: Significant hyperkalemia is stated to be due to renal failure unless proven otherwise, with aldosterone in brackets as the hormonal partner of that rule. (Book p969)

items.q: A post-operative patient on insulin infusion has a potassium of 2.9 mEq/L and a urine potassium of 8 mEq/day. Using only the two-tier rule on this page, how is this potassium level classified and why?
opts: Insignificant, because 2.5 to 3.5 is the cellular-shift band
Significant, because any value under 3.5 implies renal loss
Significant, because insulin is a listed renal toxin
Insignificant, because the low urine potassium proves renal loss
items.exp: The 2.5-3.5 mEq/L band is labelled insignificant and attributed to a cellular shift, which suits an insulin infusion, and the low urine potassium argues against renal loss. (Book p969)

items.q: Fill up: In the regulation flowchart the daily intake figure is ______ mEq, and the two exit routes given are ______ and the gastrointestinal tract.
items.exp: The tree begins with a daily intake of 100 mEq, splitting into 90-95% renal excretion and 5-10% gastrointestinal loss. (Book p969)
